extracted.intended_audience: researchers and data managers (University of the Free State and similar institutions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for researchers and data managers on implementing the FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) when creating, documenting, storing, and sharing research datasets; useful for preparing data management plans and repository submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Findable
rubrics_metrics.description: The first thing to be in place to make data reusable is the possibility to find them. It should be easy to find the data and the metadata for both humans and computers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rich metadata to provide important context for interpretation and to enable machine-based discovery. Use general or discipline-specific metadata schemes. Ensure machine-readable persistent identifiers and metadata for automatic and reliable discovery of datasets and services. Persistent identifiers unambiguously identify your data and facilitate data citation (example: Digital Object Identifier (DOI)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: The (meta)data should be retrievable by their identifier using a standardised and open communications protocol, with restrictions in place if necessary. Also, metadata should be available even when the data are no longer available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all data must be open — 'as open as possible, as closed as necessary.' Data can be restricted and still be FAIR. Keep data stored safely for the long term in an appropriate repository (general or subject-specific). Make data discoverable, describe data appropriately with metadata, and add license information. Use standard, open protocols to enable retrieval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interoperable
rubrics_metrics.description: The data should be able to be integrated with other data, applications and workflows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use open and interpretable formats so various tools can read the data; avoid proprietary software where interoperability is required. Apply interoperability at both data and metadata levels by using common formats, standards, and controlled vocabularies to enable integration across systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reusable
rubrics_metrics.description: FAIR aims at optimising the reuse of data. In order to do this, data should be well-documented, have a clear license to govern the terms of its reuse, and provenance information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide documentation such as a README to ensure correct interpretation and re-analysis. Include provenance details and contact information. Explicitly state reuse licenses to clarify terms and permissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: FAIR as guiding principles (not standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: FAIR principles are guiding principles on best practice to make data maximally reusable, but they are not standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FAIR qualities can be achieved by different standards; the principles describe how outputs should be organised for access, understanding, exchange and reuse. Use the principles to inform data management plans (DMPs) and select standards appropriate to your discipline and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess FAIRness using available tools and metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use self-assessment tools and formal metrics to assess how FAIR your data are and how to enhance them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of resources and tools: 'How FAIR are your data?' (Jones & Grootveld), F-UJI Automated FAIR Data Assessment Tool (programmatic dataset-level assessment based on FAIRsFAIR Data Object Assessment Metrics), FAIR-Aware (assesses researcher/data manager knowledge of FAIR requirements), FAIRsFAIR Data Object Assessment Metrics (lists seventeen minimum viable metrics), ACME-FAIR for research organisations, and guidance from the Australian Academy of Science. These tools help identify gaps and guide improvements to meet FAIR principles.
